![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119247/assets/fb8c2591ed5068812fa1d184d4a93a6c71b0d2ef77bb01debd4b2a03211742f7.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=2x\,i+5y\,j$ and $C$ is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $4$ respectively, traversed anticlockwise from $A(2,0)$ to $B(0,4).$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*
question.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $4$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2x\,i+5y\,j \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+20\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+20\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+20\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =72\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =72{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$
